scenarios.context: Two colleagues notice how one event is described in very different words.

speakerA.en: Look at these two headlines about the strike. One says 'Workers demand fair pay' and the other says 'Strikers paralyse the city'.
So neither headline is exactly false, but each one nudges the reader towards a conclusion.
Isn't that a bit cynical? Surely journalists simply need short, eye-catching titles.
Fair enough. I suppose the quotations they select matter just as much.
That's a useful checklist. I'll try applying it to tomorrow's front pages.
Then reading critically is less about spotting lies and more about noticing what has been left out.

speakerB.en: The facts are probably identical. It's the framing that differs, and the choice of words shapes how we feel about the event.
Precisely. That's why I always read beyond the headline and ask who benefits from a particular emphasis.
Partly, but the choice of verbs and adjectives is rarely accidental. Had the editor wanted a neutral headline, 'Transport strike begins' would have been enough.
They do. Look at who is quoted first, who gets the last word, and whose voice is missing altogether.
Do. You'll be surprised how often two reports of one event tell almost two different stories.
Well put. That's the difference between consuming the news and analysing it.

scenarios.context: Two friends follow a developing story about a factory fire.

speakerA.en: Have you seen the news about the factory fire? Some reports say it was an accident, while others suggest sabotage.
But one channel quotes an anonymous source who says the alarm system had been switched off.
Doesn't that make the news less useful? By the time it's confirmed, everyone has moved on.
That's true. A story was retracted last year, yet thousands of people had already passed it on.
So what should I do while the facts are still unclear?
That sounds sensible. I'll follow the official updates instead of the rumours.

speakerB.en: It's too early to say. With breaking news, the first reports are often incomplete, and sometimes they're simply wrong.
That's worth noting, but a single unnamed source isn't proof. I'd wait until a second source or an official investigation confirms it.
Speed and accuracy pull in opposite directions. Not only do rushed stories contain mistakes, but corrections rarely attract as much attention as the original claim.
Exactly. Were journalists more patient, there would be fewer retractions, though they might lose readers to faster websites.
Separate what has been confirmed from what is speculation, and be prepared to change your mind as new evidence emerges.
Good. And if you can't resist sharing something, at least say that it's unconfirmed.

scenarios.context: Two students discuss the likely effects of a proposed tax on sugary drinks.

speakerA.en: Did you hear that the government plans to tax sugary drinks? Supporters say it will improve public health.
The evidence from other countries suggests otherwise. Consumption fell significantly after similar taxes were introduced.
A fair objection. Were the revenue invested in school meals, though, the policy could end up benefiting those same families.
So the real question is not whether the tax works, but whether the funds are used transparently.
Which would be the best outcome. Should that happen, the tax would achieve its goal without hurting consumers.
I suppose we won't know for certain until we've seen the results over several years.

speakerB.en: In principle I agree, but I wonder whether it will change behaviour. People may simply pay more and carry on as before.
That's encouraging, but critics argue that the burden falls hardest on low-income families, who spend a larger share of their income on food.
Provided the money is spent as promised. Governments don't always keep such commitments.
Right. It would also help to know how manufacturers will react. They might reduce the sugar content rather than raise their prices.
Unless companies replace sugar with something equally unhealthy. Unintended consequences are always a risk with new legislation.
Which is why I'd like a review after two years, with the data made public.

scenarios.context: Two colleagues try to make sense of a story about inflation and interest rates.

speakerA.en: The headline says inflation has fallen to three per cent, yet prices in the shops still feel higher than ever.
So a falling rate doesn't mean things are getting cheaper.
The article also says the central bank may raise interest rates again. What's the reasoning behind that?
But doesn't that hurt people with mortgages? For some households, the cure may be worse than the disease.
I notice the article quotes only one economist. Shouldn't a balanced report include a range of views?
Then next time I'll look for analysis that compares the main arguments.

speakerB.en: That's a common misunderstanding. Inflation measures how quickly prices rise, so they can still be climbing, just more slowly.
Exactly. Prices would only fall in a period of deflation, which brings its own problems for the economy.
Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, which should reduce spending and bring prices under control.
It certainly does, and that's the dilemma. Had the economy been stronger, the bank would probably have acted more aggressively.
Ideally, yes. Economists often interpret the same figures differently, so a single expert can give a misleading impression.
A sensible approach. Figures rarely speak for themselves; they need context and careful interpretation.

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss the difference between news and commentary, and the role of a free press.

speakerA.en: I read an editorial this morning that attacked the mayor's plan. It was convincing, but is it really journalism?
The trouble is that the two often look alike online. Many readers can't tell the difference.
Some governments restrict the press altogether. Do you think that's ever justified, for example on grounds of national security?
Yet journalists have also been criticised for publishing information that put people at risk.
And with falling advertising revenue, many newspapers depend on clicks. Doesn't that encourage sensational stories?
So independent, well-funded journalism is a public good, not just a business.

speakerB.en: It's commentary, not reporting. An editorial is meant to argue a position, whereas a news report should stick to verifiable facts.
That's a real concern. Clear labels such as 'opinion' or 'analysis' would help, but not every website uses them.
Only in very narrow circumstances. Once the authorities decide what may be published, the public can no longer hold them accountable.
True, which is why responsible outlets weigh the public interest against the possible harm before they publish.
It does. The more a newspaper relies on clicks, the stronger the temptation to put drama before depth.
I'd go further: a healthy democracy can hardly function without it. Were reliable reporting to disappear, rumours would fill the gap.
